subject: biology

questions.content: What is genetic engineering?
options: Changing an organism's genes by transferring genetic material from another organism
questions.explanation: Genetic engineering is the direct modification of an organism's genome, usually by moving a gene from one organism into another so that it gains a new characteristic.

questions.content: What does GMO stand for?
questions.explanation: A GMO is a genetically modified organism: an organism whose genes have been altered using genetic engineering.

questions.content: Which of these is an example of a genetically modified crop?
options: A rose grown in a pot
Wheat grown in a field with fertiliser
An apple tree grafted onto a rootstock
questions.explanation: Golden rice has been engineered with genes so that its grains produce beta-carotene, which the body turns into vitamin A.

questions.content: Which molecule carries the genetic code in all living organisms?
questions.explanation: DNA carries the genetic instructions. Because the genetic code is universal, a gene from one species can work in another.

questions.content: Bacteria can be genetically engineered to make human insulin. Why are bacteria used?
options: They reproduce quickly and make large amounts of the protein
They are larger than human cells
They cannot be grown in a lab
questions.explanation: Bacteria divide rapidly, so a modified bacterium becomes a huge population that produces a lot of insulin in a fermenter.

questions.content: In genetic engineering, which tool is used to cut a gene out of DNA?
questions.explanation: Restriction enzymes cut DNA at specific base sequences. They are used to remove the required gene and to cut open the plasmid.

questions.content: Which enzyme joins the gene into the plasmid by sealing the DNA backbone?
questions.explanation: DNA ligase forms bonds in the sugar-phosphate backbone, joining the inserted gene to the cut plasmid to make recombinant DNA.

questions.content: What is the role of a plasmid in making human insulin in bacteria?
options: It acts as a vector that carries the human gene into the bacterial cell
questions.explanation: A plasmid is a small ring of DNA that can be taken up by bacteria. It acts as a vector, carrying the inserted gene into the host.

questions.content: Why is a gene for antibiotic resistance sometimes inserted along with the target gene into bacteria?
options: It lets scientists identify which bacteria took up the plasmid by growing them with the antibiotic
It makes the product work better
questions.explanation: Bacteria that took up the plasmid carry the resistance gene and survive on a medium containing the antibiotic, so successful cells are easy to select.

questions.content: Which is a potential benefit of herbicide-resistant GM crops?
options: Weeds can be sprayed without harming the crop
The crop makes its own herbicide
questions.explanation: The crop carries a gene that lets it tolerate a particular herbicide, so farmers can kill weeds without killing the crop and may increase yield.

questions.content: Bt maize contains a gene from the bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis. What is the advantage?
options: It makes a protein toxic to certain insect pests, reducing the need for insecticide
It makes the maize taste sweeter
It stops the maize needing soil
questions.explanation: The Bt gene makes the plant produce a toxin that harms certain caterpillars that feed on it, so less insecticide spraying is needed.

questions.content: A human gene is inserted into a sheep so that the sheep's milk contains a medicine. Which term describes this organism?
questions.explanation: A transgenic organism contains a gene from a different species. The sheep makes the human protein because the genetic code is universal.

questions.content: Which of these is a concern some people have about GM crops?
options: Genes might spread to wild relatives by cross-pollination
questions.explanation: Pollen from GM crops could pass the inserted gene to wild plants, possibly creating herbicide-resistant weeds. Concerns also include effects on other species and on biodiversity.

questions.content: Arrange the steps of making a recombinant plasmid in the correct order: (1) cut plasmid, (2) isolate gene, (3) join gene and plasmid, (4) put plasmid into bacteria.
questions.explanation: The gene is first isolated and cut out, then the plasmid is cut open, then ligase joins them, and finally the recombinant plasmid is put into bacterial cells.

questions.content: Restriction enzymes often leave short single-stranded ends called sticky ends. Why are these useful?
options: They allow complementary base pairing, so the gene and plasmid ends can join easily
questions.explanation: Sticky ends are complementary, so the gene's ends pair with the plasmid's ends by hydrogen bonding, and ligase can then seal the backbone.

questions.content: A scientist wants a crop to survive drought. Which approach is genetic engineering rather than selective breeding?
options: Inserting a drought-tolerance gene from a different species directly into the crop's DNA
Crossing the most drought-tolerant plants over many generations
questions.explanation: Genetic engineering transfers specific genes directly, even across species, and takes one generation. Selective breeding relies on existing variation and many generations.

questions.content: Which statement about the universality of the genetic code is best?
options: The same triplet codes specify the same amino acids in nearly all organisms, so a human gene can work in bacteria
Every organism has exactly the same genes
Bacteria use a different set of bases
questions.explanation: Because almost all organisms read DNA triplets as the same amino acids, a transferred gene is transcribed and translated into the same protein in the new host.

questions.content: A company claims its GM crop is safe because the inserted gene occurs naturally in another plant. Which question would best test the claim scientifically?
options: Has the crop been tested in independent, replicated trials for effects on health and the environment?
Does the company have a large advertising budget?
Is the crop a nice colour?
Does the crop have a short name?
questions.explanation: Scientific claims need evidence from independent, repeatable trials that measure specific outcomes, rather than assertions or marketing.

note:
Genetic engineering is the process of changing an organism's genome by transferring a gene from one organism to another, so that the recipient gains a new characteristic. An organism that has been changed in this way is called a genetically modified organism, or GMO. If the gene came from a different species, the organism is described as transgenic.

The process works because the genetic code is nearly universal. The same DNA triplets code for the same amino acids in almost all living things, so a gene taken from a human can be read and used by a bacterium to make a human protein.

A standard method uses bacteria to make a human protein such as insulin. First, the required gene is identified and cut out of human DNA using restriction enzymes. These enzymes cut at specific base sequences and often leave short single-stranded sticky ends. Second, a bacterial plasmid, a small ring of DNA, is cut open with the same restriction enzyme, so that it has matching sticky ends. Third, the human gene and plasmid are mixed and the enzyme DNA ligase joins them by sealing the sugar-phosphate backbone. The result is a recombinant plasmid. Fourth, the recombinant plasmids are put into bacterial cells, where the plasmid acts as a vector. The bacteria are grown in a fermenter, where they divide quickly and make large amounts of the protein, which is then extracted and purified. A marker gene, such as one for antibiotic resistance, is often included so that only the bacteria that have taken up the plasmid survive on a medium containing the antibiotic.

Genetic engineering also produces GM crops. Examples include Bt maize, which contains a bacterial gene for a toxin that harms certain insect pests, reducing the need for insecticides. Herbicide-resistant crops tolerate a weedkiller, so weeds can be controlled without harming the crop. Golden rice has been modified to make beta-carotene, which the body converts to vitamin A, to help prevent deficiency. Other examples are crops that tolerate drought, salt or frost, and tomatoes that ripen slowly and keep longer.

The benefits can include higher yields, less pesticide use, improved nutrition, and food with a longer shelf life. In medicine, engineered bacteria and animals make insulin, growth hormone and clotting factors, and genetic engineering underlies gene therapy research.

There are also concerns. Genes might spread by pollen to wild relatives, which could create herbicide-resistant weeds. Insect-resistant crops might harm non-target insects, and reliance on a single GM variety could reduce biodiversity. Some people worry about possible effects on human health, such as allergies, although approved crops are tested. Others are concerned about the cost of patented seed and the control of food supply by a few companies.

Genetic engineering differs from selective breeding. In selective breeding, individuals with desirable characteristics are chosen to reproduce over many generations, and only variation that already exists in that species can be used. Genetic engineering moves specific genes directly, even between species, and can produce a result in a single generation.

Exam tip: when describing the production of insulin, use the correct sequence and the key terms: restriction enzyme, sticky ends, plasmid, ligase, vector, recombinant DNA. When evaluating GM crops, give at least one benefit and one risk and link each to evidence.

flashcards.back: Changing an organism's genome, usually by transferring a gene from one organism to another to give a new characteristic.
An enzyme that cuts DNA at a specific base sequence, often leaving sticky ends.
An enzyme that joins DNA pieces by sealing the sugar-phosphate backbone.
A small ring of bacterial DNA used to carry a gene into a host cell.
DNA made by joining DNA from two different sources.
An organism containing a gene transferred from a different species.

flashcards.front: Why can a human gene work in bacteria?
flashcards.back: The genetic code is nearly universal, so the same triplets code for the same amino acids.
Crops with a bacterial gene for an insect toxin, reducing the need for insecticide.
Genetic engineering moves specific genes directly in one generation; selective breeding uses existing variation over many generations.

subject: biology

questions.content: What is a clone?
options: An organism genetically identical to its parent
An organism with half its genes
questions.explanation: A clone is an organism or cell with exactly the same genetic information as the one it was copied from.

questions.content: Which type of reproduction produces genetically identical offspring?
questions.explanation: Asexual reproduction involves one parent and mitosis, so offspring are genetically identical to the parent.

questions.content: Which animal was the first mammal cloned from an adult cell?
questions.explanation: Dolly the sheep, born in 1996, was cloned from a cell of an adult sheep's mammary gland.

questions.content: What is tissue culture?
options: Growing new plants from small pieces of tissue on a nutrient medium
questions.explanation: In tissue culture, small pieces of plant tissue are grown on sterile nutrient agar with hormones to produce many identical plantlets.

questions.content: Which of these is a plant cloning method used by gardeners?
questions.explanation: A cutting is a piece of stem that grows roots and becomes a new plant that is genetically identical to the parent.

questions.content: Which of these correctly describes the first step of cloning an animal by nuclear transfer?
options: The nucleus is removed from an unfertilised egg cell
An embryo is cut in half
Sperm is added to the donor cell
questions.explanation: The egg's nucleus is removed so that the egg contains no genetic material of its own. A nucleus from the donor body cell is then inserted.

questions.content: In the cloning of Dolly, which cells provided the nucleus and which provided the egg cytoplasm?
options: Nucleus from an adult udder cell; cytoplasm from an egg cell of another sheep
Nucleus from an egg; cytoplasm from an udder cell
Both from the same sheep's egg
questions.explanation: The nucleus came from a donor mammary cell of one sheep, and was inserted into an egg cell, with its nucleus removed, from a second sheep. The embryo was implanted into a third.

questions.content: Why is Dolly genetically identical to the sheep that donated the nucleus?
options: Her nuclear DNA came from the donor cell
She was fed the same food
She was born at the same time
questions.explanation: Nearly all of an organism's genetic information is in the nucleus. Dolly's nucleus came from the donor, so her nuclear DNA matched the donor's.

questions.content: Why is tissue culture carried out under sterile conditions?
options: Microbes would grow quickly on the nutrient medium and compete with or kill the plant tissue
Sterile conditions make the tissue larger
questions.explanation: The nutrient agar that supports plant tissue also supports bacteria and fungi, which would grow faster and harm the tissue.

questions.content: Which is a benefit of plant tissue culture compared with growing from seed?
options: Many identical plants can be produced quickly from a small piece of a plant with desirable features
questions.explanation: Tissue culture makes large numbers of genetically identical plants in a short time, in a small space, and can produce disease-free plants.

questions.content: What do the hormones in tissue culture medium do?
options: Stimulate cells to divide and then form roots and shoots
questions.explanation: Plant hormones such as auxins and cytokinins control cell division and differentiation, producing shoots and roots in the cultured tissue.

questions.content: Which statement correctly describes embryo transplantation in cattle?
options: An embryo is split into several parts, and each is implanted in a different surrogate cow
A sheep egg is fertilised by a human sperm
questions.explanation: In embryo splitting, an early embryo is divided into separate cells before they specialise. Each develops into a genetically identical calf in a surrogate mother.

questions.content: What is a disadvantage of cloning a whole crop population from one parent plant?
options: All the plants may be susceptible to the same disease
The plants will need no water
questions.explanation: Clones share the same genes, so if one is vulnerable to a pathogen or a change in climate, all of them are likely to be, which increases the risk of losing the whole crop.

questions.content: Stem cells are useful in medicine because they are...
options: Unspecialised and can differentiate into many cell types
questions.explanation: Stem cells can divide repeatedly and can differentiate into specialised cells, so they may be used to replace damaged tissues.

questions.content: Therapeutic cloning produces embryonic stem cells with the patient's DNA. Why is that helpful?
options: Tissues grown from them would be genetically matched, reducing rejection
They would grow faster than all other cells
questions.explanation: Cells with the patient's own DNA have the same antigens as the patient's cells, so the immune system is less likely to reject tissue grown from them.

questions.content: Cloned animals often show health problems and Dolly died younger than is typical. Which explanation might apply?
options: Cloning is inefficient and the donor nucleus may be affected by age or incorrect gene regulation
questions.explanation: Very few cloning attempts succeed. Donor nuclei may carry age-related changes and may not be reprogrammed correctly, leading to developmental problems.

questions.content: Which statement best explains why clones from the same parent plant might not look identical in different fields?
options: The environment, such as soil and light, also influences the phenotype
questions.explanation: Phenotype results from genotype and environment. Genetically identical plants can still differ in height or colour because of different light, water or nutrients.

questions.content: A rare orchid is cloned by tissue culture, and the plantlets are released into the wild. What is a limit on this conservation method?
options: Clones have little genetic variation so the population is vulnerable to disease and change
questions.explanation: Cloning can increase numbers quickly, but the population lacks genetic diversity, which is needed for adaptation and long-term survival.

note:
A clone is an organism, or a cell, that is genetically identical to another. Clones occur naturally, for example when bacteria divide by binary fission, when plants grow runners, and when identical twins form from one fertilised egg. Humans have also developed techniques to make clones on purpose.

Plant cloning. Gardeners have long used cuttings. A piece of stem is cut from a parent plant and placed in water or compost, often dipped in rooting hormone, and it grows roots to become a new plant with the same genes as the parent. Tissue culture is a more advanced method. Small pieces of tissue, or even single cells, are taken from a plant with desirable features and placed on a sterile nutrient agar medium containing plant hormones. The hormones stimulate the cells to divide, and then to form roots and shoots. The plantlets are transferred to compost. All the plants are clones of the original.

Tissue culture has several advantages. A huge number of identical plants can be produced from a tiny piece of tissue, in a small space, at any time of year. Disease-free plants can be grown from the tip of a shoot, which is often free from viruses. Rare and endangered plants can be multiplied quickly, and plants that rarely produce seeds, such as some orchids and bananas, can be propagated. The main disadvantage is that clones are genetically identical, so a disease or a change in climate could harm all of them. The method must be done in sterile conditions, because bacteria and fungi grow faster than the plant tissue on a nutrient medium.

Animal cloning. In the nuclear transfer method used to produce Dolly the sheep in 1996, an unfertilised egg cell had its nucleus removed. A nucleus from a body cell of an adult sheep was inserted into the empty egg. An electric shock stimulated the egg to start dividing, and the early embryo was implanted into a surrogate mother. The lamb born, Dolly, had the same nuclear DNA as the sheep that donated the nucleus. The success rate was very low and many attempts failed. Dolly developed arthritis and lung disease and was put down at age six, about half the usual life span, although the causes were debated.

In cattle, embryo splitting is used. An embryo from a high-quality cow and bull is divided at an early stage into several identical embryos, each of which is implanted in a surrogate cow. This produces several calves with the same genes.

Stem cells. Stem cells are unspecialised cells that can divide repeatedly and differentiate into specialised cell types. Embryonic stem cells can become almost any cell type, whereas adult stem cells, such as those in bone marrow, are more limited. Stem cells might be used to treat conditions such as damaged nerve tissue, diabetes, or blood disorders. If an embryo were cloned from the patient's own cell, the stem cells would match the patient and be less likely to be rejected, but this therapeutic cloning raises ethical questions because an embryo is destroyed.

Genotype and environment both influence the phenotype, so clones can still show differences if they grow in different conditions.

Exam tip: for a cloning question, state who provides the nucleus, who provides the egg, and who carries the embryo, and be clear which individual the clone matches genetically.

flashcards.back: An organism or cell that is genetically identical to another.
Growing many identical plantlets from small pieces of plant tissue on sterile nutrient agar with hormones.

flashcards.front: Why is tissue culture done in sterile conditions?
flashcards.back: Microbes grow quickly on the nutrient medium and would compete with or kill the plant tissue.
Remove egg nucleus, insert donor adult cell nucleus, stimulate division, implant embryo in a surrogate mother.

flashcards.front: Why is Dolly identical to the nucleus donor?
flashcards.back: Her nuclear DNA came from the donor's cell.
An early embryo is divided into several identical embryos, each placed in a surrogate mother.
An unspecialised cell that can divide and differentiate into specialised cell types.

flashcards.front: Main disadvantage of cloning a crop
flashcards.back: Low genetic variation, so all plants may be vulnerable to the same disease or environmental change.
Tissue grown from the patient's own cells is genetically matched, reducing the risk of rejection.

subject: biology

questions.content: What does the word ethics mean in science?
options: Deciding what is right or wrong in how science is used
questions.explanation: Ethics is about moral principles. In biotechnology it asks whether something should be done, not only whether it can be done.

questions.content: Which of these is an ethical concern about cloning humans?
options: It could treat people as products or harm the clone's wellbeing
questions.explanation: Reproductive cloning raises questions about identity, consent and the health and rights of the clone. Many countries ban it.

questions.content: Which group might be most concerned about the safety of GM food?
questions.explanation: Consumers eat the food, so they have a direct interest in its safety. Farmers, governments, and environmental groups are also stakeholders.

questions.content: What is a stakeholder?
options: A person or group affected by a decision
questions.explanation: Stakeholders are all those affected by or with an interest in a decision, such as patients, farmers, companies, governments, and the environment.

questions.content: Which is a benefit of using biotechnology in medicine?
options: Producing human insulin for people with diabetes
questions.explanation: Engineered bacteria make human insulin in large amounts. It is purer, cheaper and more reliable than insulin obtained from animals.

questions.content: Which is an argument in favour of GM crops?
options: They can increase yield and help feed a growing population
They always cost less to buy
questions.explanation: GM crops may be more resistant to pests, drought or disease, which could raise yields on the same land. Evidence for specific traits varies by crop and place.

questions.content: Which is an argument against patenting GM seeds?
options: Farmers may have to buy new seed every year and become dependent on a few companies
questions.explanation: Patent and licence agreements can stop farmers saving seed. Critics argue this raises costs and concentrates control of food production.

questions.content: A new GM plant is tested only in a laboratory. Why might field trials also be needed?
options: To see how it affects the real environment and other organisms
questions.explanation: Laboratory conditions cannot reproduce all real-world interactions. Field trials assess effects on non-target species, soil, gene flow and yields.

questions.content: Which statement is a fact rather than an opinion?
options: Bt maize contains a gene from Bacillus thuringiensis
GM food is unnatural and wrong
questions.explanation: The presence of the gene can be tested and verified. The other statements express values or judgements, which are opinions.

questions.content: What is the main ethical objection some people raise to embryonic stem cell research?
questions.explanation: Embryonic stem cells come from early embryos, which are destroyed in the process. People disagree about the moral status of an embryo.

questions.content: Which source of stem cells avoids the need to use embryos?
options: Adult stem cells, such as from bone marrow
questions.explanation: Adult stem cells are taken from tissues such as bone marrow. They are more limited in what they can become but do not require an embryo.

questions.content: Which is a possible environmental risk of releasing a GM crop?
options: Gene transfer to wild relatives, creating resistant weeds
questions.explanation: Cross-pollination could pass genes such as herbicide resistance to wild relatives, which might then be harder to control.

questions.content: Why do scientific bodies ask for independent peer review of biotechnology studies?
options: Other experts check the methods and conclusions for errors or bias
questions.explanation: Peer review improves reliability. Independent experts examine the design, data and conclusions before publication.

questions.content: A company funds research showing its GM crop is safe. How should you evaluate the claim?
options: Check the methods, whether results were replicated independently, and whether there is a conflict of interest
Accept it because it is a company
Reject it because companies cannot be correct
questions.explanation: Funding does not automatically invalidate research, but it is a possible source of bias. Independent replication and transparent methods give stronger confidence.

questions.content: The precautionary principle says that if an action might cause serious harm and evidence is uncertain, caution should be taken. Which action applies this principle to GM crops?
options: Delaying release until risks to health and the environment are assessed
questions.explanation: The precautionary principle favours assessment before release when serious harm is possible and uncertain, rather than waiting for harm to appear.

questions.content: Gene therapy could cure a genetic disease by altering the genes in body cells. Which issue is raised specifically if germline (egg or sperm) cells are edited?
options: Changes would be inherited by future generations who cannot consent
The treatment would be less expensive
questions.explanation: Edits to the germline are passed on, so the decision affects people who do not yet exist and cannot consent. This is why germline editing is widely regulated or banned.

questions.content: A farmer in a poorer region cannot afford patented GM seed, while a farmer in a wealthy region can. Which ethical issue does this illustrate?
options: Fairness and unequal access to the benefits of technology
questions.explanation: Cost and patents can mean that benefits of biotechnology are shared unequally, which raises questions of justice and global food security.

questions.content: Which response best shows a balanced evaluation of a biotechnology issue?
options: Weighing benefits and risks for several stakeholders using evidence, then justifying a conclusion
Stating a personal feeling without evidence
questions.explanation: A balanced evaluation considers evidence on both sides, identifies the stakeholders affected, and explains how the conclusion follows from the evidence.

note:
Biotechnology is the use of living organisms or biological processes to make products or solve problems. Genetic engineering, cloning, stem cell therapy and microbial fermentation are all examples. Science can often tell us what is possible, but deciding what should be done involves ethics, which means thinking about right and wrong, and weighing the consequences for people, other organisms and the environment.

Stakeholders. A stakeholder is a person or group affected by a decision. In a debate about a GM crop, the stakeholders could include farmers who might gain higher yields, consumers who eat the food, a company that holds the patent, environmental groups concerned about wildlife, governments that set regulations, and people in countries where food is scarce. A good evaluation considers the viewpoint of several stakeholders rather than only one.

Benefits of biotechnology. In medicine, genetically engineered bacteria make insulin, growth hormone and other proteins, which are safer and more consistent than extracts from animals. Vaccines and diagnostic tests use biotechnology. In agriculture, GM crops can be designed to resist pests, tolerate herbicides, withstand drought, or contain more nutrients. Cloning can multiply high-quality plants and animals. Stem cells offer the possibility of replacing damaged tissue.

Risks and concerns. Genes from GM crops might spread to wild relatives, and some crops might affect non-target species or reduce biodiversity. People worry about unknown long-term effects on health, although approved foods go through safety testing. Patents can make farmers dependent on companies for seed. For cloning, there are concerns about the low success rate, animal welfare, loss of genetic diversity and, for humans, identity and consent. Embryonic stem cell research is opposed by some because the embryo is destroyed, whereas adult stem cells avoid this but are more limited. If germline cells are edited, changes would be inherited by future generations, who cannot consent.

Evidence, fact and opinion. A fact can be checked with evidence, such as the statement that a crop contains a given gene. An opinion is a judgement, such as the statement that GM food is unnatural. Both are part of debate, but only evidence can settle factual questions. When judging a source, ask who produced it, who paid for it, whether the method is clear, whether results were repeated by independent scientists, and whether it has been peer reviewed. Possible bias, such as a conflict of interest, should be considered but does not automatically mean the data are wrong.

Regulation and the precautionary principle. Governments regulate biotechnology through safety tests, field trials and labelling. The precautionary principle says that when an action could cause serious harm and the evidence is uncertain, caution should be taken before going ahead. Other people argue that excessive caution can delay useful technology and the benefits it might bring, so regulation often tries to balance both.

Fairness and access. New technologies can be expensive. If only wealthy countries or farmers can afford them, benefits are shared unequally. Ethical discussions therefore also include justice, cost and global food security.

Exam tip: for a discuss or evaluate question, give at least two arguments on each side, name the stakeholders, use a piece of evidence or an example, and finish with a justified conclusion rather than just a list.

flashcards.back: Using living organisms or biological processes to make products or solve problems.
Thinking about what is right and wrong, and weighing consequences for people and the environment.
A person or group affected by, or interested in, a decision.
A fact can be checked with evidence; an opinion is a personal judgement.
If an action might cause serious harm and evidence is uncertain, take caution before proceeding.

flashcards.front: Environmental risk of a GM crop
flashcards.back: Genes could spread to wild relatives, and non-target species or biodiversity could be affected.
Farmers may depend on a few companies and have to buy seed each season.
Changes are inherited by future generations, who cannot consent.
Check who made and funded it, whether methods are clear, whether results were repeated independently, and whether it was peer reviewed.
